en: The Glorious Thousand-Name Hymn to Śiva (Śrīśivasahasranāmastotram)

I bow to Śambhu, the lord of Umā; I bow to the preceptor of the gods; I bow to the cause of the universe; I bow to the one adorned with serpents and the bearer of the deer; I bow to the Lord of creatures.
I bow to the one whose eyes are the sun, the moon, and fire; I bow to the beloved of Mukunda.
I bow to the refuge of devotees and I bow to Śiva, the bestower of boons;
O my dear Yudhiṣṭhira, thereafter Vāsudeva, having become composed, [spoke].
With palms joined in reverence, Upamanyu spoke from the beginning a compendium of the names of the Brahmin-sages:
"By means of those proclaimed by Brahmā, those proclaimed by the ṛṣis, and those originating from the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas..."
I shall praise with names Him who is renowned throughout all the worlds and worthy of praise—
names that are great, established, true, perfected, and accomplishing all purposes,
composed with devotion by the seer Taṇḍi, whose soul was made one with the Vedas.
As it was proclaimed by the virtuous, renowned sages who perceive reality—
excellent, foremost, leading to heaven, beneficial to all beings, and auspicious—
and as it has been heard everywhere in the world, brought down from the realm of Brahmā.
I shall declare that supreme, eternal Brahman as proclaimed by Brahmā through the truths;
listen to me with focused attention, O best of the Yadu clan.
Choose this Lord Bhava, the Supreme Ishvara, as your object of devotion.
Therefore, I shall cause you to hear that which is the eternal Brahman;
it is not possible for anyone to describe the entirety of Śarva’s manifestations in detail,
even by one who is disciplined, even in hundreds of years.
O Mādhava, who could possibly describe in their entirety the qualities of Him whose beginning, middle, and end cannot be grasped even by the gods? Nevertheless,
I shall speak of that Great Lord in brief, using words and syllables of concise meaning.
I shall describe his conduct according to my ability, through the grace of that wise one;
for without having obtained his permission, it is not possible to praise the Lord.
When he was indeed permitted by him, then was he praised by me.
I shall declare a brief enumeration of the names of that Great Soul, whose origin is unmanifest, who is without beginning or end, the source of the world,
the giver of boons, the most excellent, whose form is the universe, and who is wise.
Listen, O Kṛṣṇa, to this collection of names which was spoken by the Lotus-born;
those ten thousand names which the Great-Grandfather proclaimed, having churned them with my mind, I have extracted like butter from curd. (13)
Just as gold is the essence of ore, as honey is the essence of flowers,
and as the scum is the essence of clarified butter— so has this essence been extracted from that [work].
It removes all sins and is endowed with the four Vedas.
It should be acquired with effort and retained by one of disciplined mind;
it is auspicious, nourishing, a destroyer of demons, purifying, and great.
This should be given to a devotee who possesses faith and is not an atheist.
Not to one who is faithless, nor to an atheist whose self is unsubdued;
nor to one who finds fault with the Lord, the God who is the causal Self—O Kṛṣṇa, such a person goes to hell along with his ancestors and his offspring. (17–18)
This is meditation, this is yoga, and this is the unsurpassed object of meditation;
this is that which is to be chanted, this is knowledge, and this is the supreme secret.
By knowing this, one shall indeed attain the highest goal even at the time of death.
This is pure, auspicious, holy, and this most excellent blessing.
In ancient times, Brahmā, the grandfather of all the worlds, having composed this,
ordained it as the sovereign king among all divine hymns of praise.
From that time forth, this hymn to the Great-Souled Īśvara became renowned in the world as the "King of Hymns" (Stavarāja), worshipped by the immortals.
This King of Hymns was brought down from the world of Brahmā into heaven.
Because Taṇḍi obtained it in ancient times, it became known as the *Taṇḍikṛta*.
Indeed, by means of Taṇḍi, heaven was brought down here to the world of mortals;
it is the most auspicious of all auspicious things and the destroyer of all sins.
O mighty-armed one, I shall proclaim this hymn, the best among all hymns—
that which is the Brahman even of the Brahmanas, that which is the Supreme even of the supreme;
that which is the splendor even of all splendors, and that which is the austerity even of all austerities.
He who is the peace of those who are peaceful, the splendor of those who possess splendor;
he who is the self-control of those who are self-controlled, and the wisdom of those who are wise;
he who is the god of even the gods, and the seer of even the seers. (26–27)
He who is the sacrifice among sacrifices, who is Śiva even among the auspicious ones,
who is Rudra among the Rudras, and who is the splendor even of those possessing splendor;
he who is the yogi among yogis and the cause of all causes.
From whom the worlds arise and into whom they cease to be—
listen to me as I recite the one thousand and eight names of Hara, who is the self of all beings and possesses immeasurable splendor. (29–30)
Having heard this, O tiger among men, you shall obtain all your desires:
he who is Steadfast, the Motionless One, the Lord, the Terrible, the Most Excellent, the Giver of Boons, the Best;
the Soul of All, the Renowned by All, the All, the Maker of All, and Bhava.
He has matted hair, wears a deer skin, and bears a crest; he is the one who animates all limbs and the creator of all beings. He is Hara, the fawn-eyed one, the Lord who withdraws all creatures.
He is worldly activity and its cessation, the self-restrained, the eternal, and the immutable.
The Blessed One dwells in the cremation ground; he moves through the sky, he is the destroyer, and he is to be saluted.
He performs great deeds, he is an ascetic, and he is the creator of all beings. He appears in the guise of a madman, yet he remains concealed as the Lord of all worlds and progenitors.
He of great form and great body, bull-like in appearance and of great renown;
the Great-Souled One, the Self of all beings, whose form is the universe and who has mighty jaws; the Guardian of the World, the hidden Self, the Graceful One, blue-and-red in hue. ||35-36||
He is the purifier and the great one; he is the observance and the one who relies upon observances.
He is the performer of all actions, the self-existent, the beginning, the first creator, and the treasure-house.
He is the thousand-eyed, the large-eyed, the moon, and the accomplisher of the constellations.

He is the moon, the sun, Saturn, Ketu, the planet, the lord of planets, and the most excellent; he is the beginning, the end, and dissolution; the creator; the one who delivers the deer and the arrow; the sinless one;
possessed of great austerity and terrible austerity; the undepressed one; and the achiever for the distressed.
He is the mantra that brings about the year, the supreme authority, and the highest austerity;
he is the one to be united through yoga, the great seed, the one of great virility, and the one of great strength.
He is the one whose seed is gold, the omniscient, the excellent seed, and the one who carries the seed.
The ten-armed one, the unblinking, the blue-throated, the lord of Umā;
the universal form, the self-superior, the strong hero, Bala, the Gaṇa;
the creator of the Gaṇas, the lord of the Gaṇas, the sky-clad, and indeed Kāma himself.
The supreme knower of mantras, the mantra itself, the creator of all beings, and the destroyer;
bearing a water-pot, wielding a bow, with arrows in hand and carrying a skull-cup;
armed with the thunderbolt, the *śataghnī*, the sword, and the *paṭṭiśa*—he is the great wielder of weapons.
Suvahasta, Surūpa, Tejas, Tejaskara, Nidhi,
Uṣṇīṣin, Suvaktra, Udagra, Vinata, Dīrgha, Harikeśa, Sutīrtha, and Kṛṣṇa. ||44-45||
Siddhārtha in the form of a jackal, the shaven-headed one who brings all auspiciousness;
the unborn, the multiformed, the bearer of the Gaṅgā, and the one with matted hair;
he whose vital energy flows upward, whose phallus is erect, who sleeps in a supine position, and whose abode is the sky.
Trijata, Chiravasa, Rudra, the all-pervading Senapati;
Naktañcara, Ahaścara, Tigmamanyu, Suvarcas;
Gajahā, Daityahā, Kāla, Lokadhātṛ, and Guṇākara. ||47-48||
He has the form of a lion and a tiger, and is clothed in a tiger skin;
he is the Yogi of Time, the Great Lord, the fulfiller of all desires, and the one at the crossroads.
He is the night-walker, the king of the spirits, the wanderer among beings, and the Great Sovereign.
He has become manifold, the sustainer of many, the sun-eclipsing Rahu, and one whose movement is immeasurable.
He is fond of dance, eternally dancing, a dancer, and full of grace.
He is a hero of most formidable asceticism, eternal, free from desire, and without abode.
Sahasrahasta, Vijaya, Vyavasāya, Atandrita,
Amarṣaṇa, Amarṣaṇātman, Yajñaha, Kāmanāśaka,
Dakṣayāgāpahārī, Susaha, and likewise Madhyama.
He who takes away splendor, the destroyer of strength, the joyful one, the purposeful, the unconquered, the excellent;
he whose roar is deep, the profound one, the one possessing deep power and vehicles;
he whose form is like the banyan tree, who stands with ears like the banyan tree, the all-pervading Lord.
He has very sharp teeth, a massive body, and a great mouth;
he is Viṣvaksena, the sacrifice of Hari, whose vehicle is the Saṃyugāpīḍa elephant.
He is Tīkṣṇatāpa, Haryaśva, the companion who knows the proper time for action.
He is the sacrifice propitiated by Viṣṇu, the ocean, and the submarine fire (vaḍavāmukha).
He is the companion of the consumer of oblations (Agni), the one whose self is tranquil, the consumer of oblations,
the one of fierce splendor, the one of great splendor, the one who is to be produced, and the knower of the time for victory.

The course of the luminaries, accomplishment, and indeed the embodiment of all forms; the crested, the shaven-headed, the matted-haired, the flaming, the one born of form, the one dwelling on the head, the powerful;
the devotee of Viṣṇu, the swift, the palm-clapper, the playful, and the one who is formidable as Death.
Nakṣatravigrahamati, Guṇabuddhi, Layāgama; Prajāpati, Viśvabāhu, Vibhāga, Sarvatomukha;
Vimocana, Sumaraṇa, and Hiraṇyakavacodbhava. || 59–60 ||
Meghaja, Balacārī, Mahīcārī, and likewise Stuta;
Sarvatūryavinodī, and Sarvavādyaparigraha; Vyālarūpa, Guhāvāsī, Grahāmālī, and Taraṅgavid.
Tridaśa, who liberates from all bonds of time, vision, and karma;
Bandhana, the destroyer of enemies in battle against the lords of the asuras;
Sāṃkhyaprasāda, Durvāsas, who is served by all the virtuous. || 62-63 ||
Praskandana, the knower of distinctions, the incomparable one who knows the portions of sacrifice;
Sarvavāsa, the wanderer everywhere, Durvāsas, Vāsava, and the immortal;
Haima, Hemakara, the Sacrifice, the sustainer of all, and the best of sustainers.
Lohitākṣa, Mahākṣa, Vijayākṣa, Viśārada;
Saṃgraha, Nigraha, Kartṛ, Sarpacīranivāsana; Mukhya, Amukhya, Deha, Kāhali, and Sarvakāmada.
He is constant faith, possessed of great strength, and the bearer of power and form;
he is the granter of all desires, the giver of everything, and faces in every direction.
He is the formless void, the inevitable fall, and the bird that moves through the sky.
The fierce-formed Aṃśu, Āditya, the one with many rays, the most resplendent;
Vasuvega, Mahāvega, Manovega, the night-walker;
the dweller in all, the abode of Śrī, the giver of instruction, and the handless one.
The Sage, the Self, the Lightless, and the Breaker of the Thousandfold; the Bird, the Form of the Plakṣa tree, the Exceedingly Radiant, and the Lord of the People. 70.
Intoxication, Madana, Desire, the Holy Fig Tree, the Bestower of Wealth, and Glory.
Vāmadeva, Vāma, facing east, south, and north;
Siddhayogī, Maharṣi, Siddhārtha, Siddhasādhaka;
Bhikṣu, Bhikṣurūpa, Vipaga, Mṛdu, and Avyaya.
Mahāsena, Viśākha, the Lord of Cows who is the sixtieth part,
Vajrahasta, Viṣkambhin, and Camūstambhana;
Vṛttavṛttakara, Tāla, Madhu, and Madhukalocana.
The Lord of Speech, the winner of booty, eternally honored by those who have sought his refuge;
the celibate student, the wanderer of the world, the all-pervading, the knower of discernment;
the Ruler, the Sovereign, Time, the night-walker, the bearer of the Pināka bow.
He who abides in signs and is the sign itself; he who is joy, the creator of joy, and Hari;
Nandīśvara, Nandin, the Delighter, and the Increaser of Joy;
the Remover of Fortune, the Destroyer, Time, Brahmā, and the Grandfather.
The four-faced one, the great linga, and likewise the beautiful linga;
the presiding lord of the lingas, the presiding lord of the gods, the presiding lord of yoga, the bringer of light;
the presiding lord of the seed, the creator of the seed, the one who has entered into the supreme self, and the powerful one.
Itihāsa, Sakalpa, Gautama, Niśākara, Dambha, Adambha, Vaidambha, Vaśya, Vaśakara, Kali,
Lokakartṛ, Paśupati, Mahākartṛ, and Anauṣadha.
The imperishable, the supreme Brahman, the powerful, and indeed the capable;
policy and non-policy, the pure-minded, the pure, the venerable, and he who has gone and returned;
he of many favors, the one of auspicious dreams, the mirror, and you, the conqueror of enemies.
The author of the Vedas, the creator of mantras, the wise one, the crusher of armies;
he who dwells in great clouds, the most terrible, the subduer;
the flame of fire, the great blaze, the deep smoky one, the oblation, the sacrificial offering.
Vṛṣabha, Śaṅkara, Nitya, Varcasvin, Dhūmaketana;
83 Nīla, Aṅgalubdha, Śobhana, Niravagraha;
Svastida, Svastibhāga, Bhāgin, Bhāgakara, and Laghu. 84
Utsaṅga, Mahāṅga, and Mahāgarbhaparāyaṇa;
Kṛṣṇavarṇa and Suvarṇa, the sense-organ of all embodied beings;
Mahāpāda, Mahāhasta, Mahākāya, and Mahāyaśas.
He has a great head, great measures, and great eyes; his abode is the night.
He is the Great Destroyer, with great ears, great lips, and great jaws.
He has a great nose, a great throat, a great neck, and he dwells in the cremation ground.
He has a broad chest and a wide breast; he is the inner self and the abode of wild beasts.
He is the one who hangs down, the one with hanging lips, the master of great illusion, and the ocean of milk.
He has great teeth, great tusks, a great tongue, and a great mouth.
Mahānakhah (Great Nail), Mahāromā (Great Hair), Mahākeśaḥ (Great Hairs), Mahājaṭaḥ (Great Matted Locks);

Prasannaḥ (The Serene), Prasādaḥ (Grace), Pratyayaḥ (Conviction), Girisādhanaḥ (Accomplisher of the Mountain); Snehanaḥ (The Gladdener) and Asnehanaḥ (The Non-Gladdener), as well as Ajitaḥ (The Unconquered), the Great Sage. || 89-90 ||
He whose form is a tree, whose banner is a tree, who is fire, whose vehicle is the wind;
he who is Gaṇḍalī, whose abode is Mount Meru, and who is the Lord of the Gods.
He whose head is the Atharvaveda, whose mouth is the Sāmaveda, and whose eyes are as immeasurable as a thousand Ṛgvedic verses.
He whose feet and arms are the Yajus; the secret one; the manifest one; likewise, the moving one (92).
He whose purpose is unfailing; grace; the one who is approachable; the beautiful to behold (93).
The benefactor; the beloved; the all-encompassing; the golden one; he whose complexion is like gold.
The navel, the joy-inducing state, the architect of the lotus, the steadfast one;
the first of the twelve seats, the sacrifice, and he who is absorbed in sacrifice.
Night, the Kali age, time, the crocodile, and he who is worshipped by Time.
He who is with his retinue, the creator of the Gaṇas, whose charioteer is Bhūtavāhana;
he whose abode is ashes, the protector of ashes, who has become the ash-tree, the Gaṇa;
the guardian of the world, as well as the world itself, the Great Soul honored by all.
Pure, endowed with the three-fold whiteness, frequented by beings,
established in the stages of life, grounded in ritual action, possessing a mind like that of Viśvakarman, excellent,
with broad branches, copper-colored lips, a webbed lotus-like hand, and perfectly steady— (97) [he was like a tree].
Kapila, Kapiśa, Śukla, Āyu, Para, Apara;
Gandharva, Aditi, Tārkṣya, Suvijñeya, Suśārada; the god whose weapon is the paraśvadha, Anukārī, and Subāndhava. || 98–99 ||

He who holds a lute made of a gourd, the Great Wrathful One, whose vital energy flows upward, who reclines upon the waters; the Fierce One, the Maker of Subservience, the Lineage, the Sound of the Lineage, indeed the Irreproachable;
He whose form is all limbs, the Master of Illusion, the Friend, the Wind, and the Fire.
The binder and the creator of bonds, the liberator from firm fetters; he is the seeker of sacrifice, the seeker of desire, the one with great tusks, and the wielder of great weapons;
he is the blameless one in many forms, the benefactor of all, and the moon-crested lord.
Amareśa, Mahādeva, Viśvadeva, Surārihā,
Ahibudhnya, Anilābha, Cekitāna, and likewise Hari;
Ajaikapād, Kāpālī, Triśaṅku, Ajita, and Śiśu.
Dhanvantari, Dhūmaketu, Skanda, and Vaiśravaṇa;
Dhātṛ, Śakra, Viṣṇu, Mitra, Tvaṣṭṛ, Dhruva, Dhara, Prabhāva, Sarvaga, Vāyu, Aryaman, Savitṛ, and Ravi. || 104–105 ||
Uṣaṅgu, Vidhātṛ, Māndhātṛ, Bhūtabhāvana, Vibhu, Varṇavibhāvī, and Sarvakāmaguṇāvaha;
Padmanābha, Mahāgarbha, Candravaktra, Anila, and Anala. || 106 ||
He is powerful and tranquil, ancient and renowned for his merit;
he is the creator of the Kurus, the dweller among the Kurus, one who has become the Kuru lineage, and the medicine of all virtues.
He is the intention of all, the one who moves upon darbha grass, and the Lord of all living beings.
The god of gods, devoted to bliss, the knower of all jewels, both existent and non-existent;
he who dwells on Mount Kailāsa and takes refuge in the Himavat mountains;
the destroyer of banks and the maker of banks, possessed of manifold knowledge and a giver of much.
The merchant, the carpenter, the tree, the *vakula* flower, and the sandalwood-leaved;
the one with a strong neck, the great collarbone, the unshakable, and the great medicine;
the accomplisher of goals, the successful one, and the one who excels in prosody and grammar. (110–111)
He who has the lion’s roar, the lion’s fangs, the lion’s speed, and the lion as his vehicle;

whose essence is power, who is the time of the world, the destroyer of time, the one who benefits the world, the one who is the essence, whose body is the new wheel, who wears a garland of banners, and who is accompanied by Bhāvanā. 112.
The abode of beings, the lord of beings, the blameless one throughout day and night;
he who has caused all beings to increase, the universal refuge, the pervasive Bhava; the unerring, the self-restrained, the horse, the nourisher, and the sustainer of life. ||113-114||
Dhṛtimān, Matimān, Dakṣa, Satkṛta, and Yugādhipa;
Gopālī, Gopati, Grāma, Gocarmavasana, and Hari;
Hiraṇyabāhu, as well as Guhāpāla and Praveśaka.
Prakṛṣṭāri, Mahāharṣa, Jitakāma, Jitendriya,
Gāndhāra, Suvāsa, Tapassakta, Ratinara, Mahāgīta, Mahānṛtya, and he who is served by hosts of Apsarases. 116–117.
The great banner, the great element, moving with many followers;
he who is to be made known, the possession, the bringer of happiness through all fragrances.
He is the archway, the deliverer, the wind, the lord of the enclosure, and the sky-walker.
He is union, the increaser, the grown, the exceedingly grown, and the one possessed of superior qualities;
he is the eternal self, the companion, the lord of gods and asuras, and the master; he is the joined one, the one with joined arms, the god of the gods in heaven, and the one with beautiful joints.
Āṣāḍha, Suṣāḍha, Dhruva, Hariṇa, Hara,
Vapu, Āvartamāna, Vasuśreṣṭha, Mahāpatha,
Śirohārī, Vimarśa, and he who is marked with all auspicious characteristics.
He is the axle and the one who yokes the chariot; he is the master of all yoga and possesses great strength.
He is the sacred tradition and that which is beyond the tradition; he is the deity of the holy fords and the great charioteer.
He is the lifeless and the giver of life; he is the mantra and the auspicious-eyed one; he is exceedingly firm.
Born of jewels, red-limbed, he knows the great oceans and the channels of water; he is the root, vast, immortal, manifest and unmanifest, a treasure-house of austerity;
he is the ascent and the further ascent, the upholder of virtue, and of great fame.
In the *Senākalpa* and the *Mahākalpa*, he is Yoga, the performer of yoga, and Hari;
he is the form of the ages (*yuga*), the one of great form, the slayer of the great serpent, and the destroyer.
He is the bestower of justice, the foot, the wise one, and indeed like a mountain.
Bahumāla, Mahāmāla, Śaśin, Harisulocana,
Vistāra, Lavaṇa, Kūpa, Triyuga, Saphalodaya,
Trilocana, Viṣaṇṇāṅga, Maṇividdha, and Jaṭādhara.
Bindu, Visarga, Sumukha, Śara, Sarvāyudha,
Saha, Nivedana, Sukhājāta, Sugandhāra, Mahādhanus,
Gandhapālī, Bhagavat, and Utthāna, the source of all actions. (128–129)
The churning-stick is the pervasive wind; he is the whole, the all-seeing.
He is the palm, the hand, the vessel, and the great one with upward-knit body.
He is the parasol, the well-canopied, the renowned world, the refuge of all, and the cosmic order.
Shaven-headed, deformed, and distorted, he carries a staff and a water-pot; he is the performer of transformations.
He has tawny eyes, is the direction itself, wields the thunderbolt, possesses a hundred tongues and a thousand feet.
With a thousand heads, he is the lord of gods, the embodiment of all deities, and the supreme teacher.
He who has a thousand arms and all limbs, the refuge of all, the creator of all worlds;
he who is the purifier, the mantra Trikakud, the youngest, and dark-brown in hue;
the fashioner of Brahmā’s staff, and the wielder of the Śataghnī, the noose, and the spear.
The one whose essence is the lotus, the great essence, the essence of Brahman, the one born from the waters;
the ray of light, the creator of Brahman, Brahman, the knower of Brahman, the Brāhmaṇa, the goal;
the one of infinite forms, the single self, the fiercely radiant, the self-existent.
The self that ascends is Paśupati, possessing the speed of the wind and the swiftness of thought;
he is the one who is fragrant with sandalwood, who crosses over by means of the tip of a lotus stalk, and who is the supreme man.
Wearing a great garland of *karṇikāra* flowers, with a dark-blue crest, he is the wielder of the Pināka bow.
Lord of Umā, beloved of Umā, bearer of the Gaṅgā, and the consort of Umā;
the Excellent One, the Boar, the Giver of Boons, the Most Worthy, and the One of Great Sound; the One of Great Grace, the Subduer, the Destroyer of Foes, and the White-Tawny One. ||137-138||
He whose soul is joyful, who is the Supreme Soul, whose self is disciplined, and who upholds the primary matter;
he who is blissful on all sides, the three-eyed one, the common ground of Dharma, and the most excellent;
he who is the soul of the moving and the unmoving, the subtle soul, the immortal, and the Lord of the Bull.
Sādhya, Ṛṣi, Vasu, Āditya, Vivasvat, Savitṛ, and Amṛta;
Vyāsa, Sarga, Susaṅkṣepa, Vistara, Paryaya, and Nara;
Ṛtu, Saṃvatsara, Māsa, Pakṣa, and Saṃkhyāsamāpana. ||140-141||
He is the divisions of time—kalā, kāṣṭhā, lava, mātrā, muhūrta, day, night, and moments;
the field of the universe, the seed of progeny, the primordial mark, and the one who is most difficult to transcend.
He is being and non-being, the manifest and the unmanifest, the father, the mother, and the grandfather.
The gateway to heaven, the gateway to progeny, the gateway to liberation, and the triple-heaven;
Nirvāṇa, the source of delight, the world of Brahmā, and the supreme goal;
the creator of gods and asuras, and the ultimate refuge of gods and asuras.
The god who is the teacher of gods and asuras, honored by gods and asuras;
the great minister of gods and asuras, the refuge of the hosts of gods and asuras;
the presiding lord over the hosts of gods and asuras, the leader of the hosts of gods and asuras. 145.
The god of gods, the divine seer, the bestower of boons upon gods and asuras;
the lord of gods and asuras, the universal one, the great sovereign of gods and asuras;
composed of all the gods, inconceivable, the self of the deities, born of the Self. 146–147.
Ūdbhid, Trivikrama, Vaidya, Viraja, Nīraja, Amara;
the one worthy of praise (Īḍya), Hastīśvara, Vyāghra, Devasiṃha, Nararṣabha;
Vibudha, Agravara, Sūkṣma, Sarvadeva, and Tapomaya. || 148 ||
Well-yoked, beautiful, wielder of the thunderbolt, the source of spears, and imperishable;
Guha, the beloved, the innate creation, the pure one, the purifier of all;
the horned one, lover of horns, tawny-hued, king of kings, and free from disease.
He who is the delight of the hosts of gods, the cessation of all worldly means,
whose eye is on his forehead, the god of the universe, the golden-hued one, and the splendor of Brahman;
he who is the lord of stationary beings and the one who increases self-restraint and the senses.
Siddhārtha, Siddhabhūtārtha, Acintya, Satyavrata, Śuci;
Vratādhipa, Paraṃbrahma, Bhaktānugrahakāraka; Vimukta, Muktatejas, Śrīmān, and Śrīvardhana of the world. ||152-153||
Thus have I praised the Blessed One with devotion according to his preeminence—he whom neither the gods, beginning with Brahmā, nor the sages know in truth.
Who can praise the Lord of the World, who is to be praised, worshipped, and revered? (154)

Thus, having placed the all-pervading Lord of Sacrifice before me with devotion, I then obtained his permission and praised that best among the wise. Praising the auspicious God with these names that increase prosperity, I extolled him. (155-156)
Ever disciplined and pure, he attains the Self by means of the self;
for this is the supreme Brahman, and through it one reaches the supreme Brahman.
The seers and the gods, devoted to that, praise it with these words.
When praised by those of self-restraint, Mahādeva is pleased;
the Lord is compassionate toward his devotees, the all-pervading one who establishes [them] in his own self.
And likewise among men, those men who are preeminent—‖ 158–159‖
The believers, full of faith, through praises over many births,
with devotion and with undivided mind, [worship] the Lord, the supreme,
eternal God of immeasurable splendor, by deed, thought, word, and inner feeling. (160)
Whether lying down or waking, walking or sitting, opening their eyes or closing them, they think of Bhava again and again;
they hear of him, cause others to hear of him, and speak of him. (161–162)
Praising and being praised, they are satisfied and delighted;

for a living being whose sins have been removed, devotion arises in this world throughout thousands of millions of births across various wombs of saṃsāra. (163) Devotion is born in one who is free from evil.
And may there arise within me a devotion toward him that is exclusive and total in every respect. Furthermore, he is the eternal cause of this liberated one;
such [devotion] is difficult to attain among the gods and is not found among men.
Undisturbed and stainless devotion to Rudra is unswerving;
and by his grace alone does such devotion arise in men, by which those whose minds are absorbed in that state attain supreme perfection. (166)

Those who, following all states of being, take refuge in Maheśvara—may that God, who is affectionate toward those who seek refuge, deliver them from the cycle of worldly existence (saṃsāra). Other gods do not provide such liberation from saṃsāra in this way. (167–168)
"O Lord, for human beings there is no power other than the strength of austerity.
Thus, O Kṛṣṇa, was the Blessed One— the Lord of both the existent and the non-existent, clad in an elephant hide— praised by the auspicious-minded Tāṇḍin, who was like Indra himself.
Brahmā himself memorized this hymn to the Blessed One.
Let it be sung so that he may be awakened in the presence of Brahmā and Śaṅkara;
for this is meritorious, purifying, and always a destroyer of sin.
It bestows yoga, liberation, heaven, and likewise satisfaction;
those who recite this with single-minded devotion to Śaṅkara attain that same goal which belongs to the followers of Sāṃkhya and Yoga. (172)
A devotee who recites this hymn with diligence for one year in the presence of Rudra shall obtain his desired fruit.
This is the supreme secret, established within the heart of Brahmā.
Brahmā spoke it to Śakra; Śakra spoke it to Mṛtyu;
Mṛtyu spoke it to the Rudras; from the Rudras it came to Taṇḍi.
It was obtained by Taṇḍi in the abode of Brahmā through great austerity.
Tandi spoke it to Śukra, and Bhārgava spoke it to Gautama;
O Mādhava, Gautama spoke it to Vaivasvata Manu, and Manu spoke it to the wise and beloved Sādhya Nārāyaṇa. || 176-177 ||
The blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa, the infallible Sādhya, spoke it to Yama; the blessed Vaivasvata Yama spoke it to Nāciketa;
and O Vārṣṇeya, Nāciketa declared it to Mārkaṇḍeya.
O Janārdana, I have obtained this from Mārkaṇḍeya through the observance of religious discipline.
O slayer of enemies, I shall indeed give you this hitherto unknown hymn of praise,
which leads to heaven, bestows health and long life, brings prosperity, and is equal in merit to the Vedas.
Neither Dānavas, Yakṣas, nor Rākṣasas, nor Piśācas, Yātudhānas, Guhyakas, or even Bhujangas can create obstacles for him.
O Pārtha, he who, being pure, a celibate student, and having conquered his senses,
recites this with unbroken yoga for a year, shall obtain the fruit of a horse sacrifice.
Thus ends the section on the Dharma of Giving within the Anuśāsana Parva of the glorious Mahābhārata.
The seventeenth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Jewel-like Hymn of the Thousand Names of Śrī Śiva," is concluded.
The Jewel-like Hymn of the Thousand Names of Śrī Śiva is complete.
